                 SEGMENT I1 LANDOWNERS INITIAL BRIEF – PARTY NO. 471

           COMES NOW Segment i1 Landowners1 (“Landowners”), Party No. 471 in SOAH
Order No. 31, and files this Initial Brief in this docket. Segment i1 Landowners consist of property
owners whose land is directly affected by potential routes for a proposed 765-kV transmission line
and related facilities (“Project”) in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason,
McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties,
Texas project proposed by the joint application (“Application”) of Oncor Electric Delivery
Company LLC (“Oncor”) and the LCRA Transmission Services Corporation (collectively
“Applicants”) to amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity for authority to develop,
own and operate the Project. In sum, regarding the proposed route that best meets the applicable
statutory and Commission requirements, Landowners support the recommendation of the two
parties in this case that are the most qualified to conduct the required in-depth analyses for this
process and the only parties disinterested in the location of the proposed facilities other than
compliance with applicable standards: the Applicants, for Route 894, and Commission Staff, for
Route 487. Regarding Route Segment i1, Landowners have also shown that this segment is
unsuitable for use as a transmission line route, as explained in its testimony admitted into evidence
in the docket, Segment i1 Landowners Exhibits 1 and 2.


1
    Incorporated as a non-profit corporation in the State of Texas.


                                                             2
         Landowners greatly appreciate the professional approach the State Office of
Administrative Hearings (“SOAH”) Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) employed during the
hearing on the merits in this proceeding, in particular making reasonable accommodations and
constructive procedures and rulings to accommodate the very large number of parties not
represented by counsel, who are dealing with processes that can be challenging and confusing to
those not accustomed to these proceedings. The ALJs managed several hundred participating
parties, addressed complex issues, made difficult evidentiary and other rulings with clarity, and
kept order and forward progress for an efficient hearing. At the conclusion of the hearing, many
parties participating expressed well-deserved appreciation for the ALJ’s effectiveness and
efficiency in conducting this very difficult proceeding, to which Landowners wholeheartedly join.

                         I.      DISINTERESTED PARTIES ON ROUTE

        The record in this case will surely be one of the most voluminous in the history of SOAH
with literally thousands of filings in the docket inclusive of several hundred sets of testimony and
other filings and other documents that landed in the evidentiary record. This along with the
extraordinarily short timeframe the ALJs must meet to provide the Commission a Proposal for
Decision (“PFD”) in time for a Commission decision by September 22, 2026, will be an immense
and unprecedented task.         Of course, transmission line CCN proceedings are notoriously
contentious as landowners and those that live in the areas affected by new transmission lines are
very motivated to prevent these projects from coming into their communities. Not to mention that
many other factors that must be considered such as environmental impacts, affects to community
values, and impacts to sites of historic and prehistoric significance.

        The intervenors advocating for a particular route in this case are motivated by their interest
and preference to not have a transmission line located on or near them. This is certainly an
understandable motivation for engagement in this process, but it must be acknowledged there is
an inherent bias in the advocacy for the ultimate route selection in the recommendation by the
ALJs. However, there are two parties that are solely motivated by the legal obligation to comply
with the requirements and standards set forth in the Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) and
Commission’s rules.2 Those are the Applicants and the Commission Staff.


2
 Texas Utilities Code, Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) 37.056(c)(4)(A)–(D); 16 Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”)
25.101.


                                                      3
         Both of these parties are highly experienced and deeply versed in the requirements of the
Commission in these CCN transmission cases including the application of the standards to
proposed projects like the transmission project in this docket.                 Casey D. Petty, an Oncor
representative, describes how Route 894 is the route that best meets those requirements.3 Mr. Petty
is a highly experienced transmission planning engineer with over 18 years of experience.4 In
reaching his recommendation, Mr. Petty relied on extensive analyses and inputs provided by expert
resources and Applicants’ other witnesses that are independent of any routing preferences,
including the Environmental Assessment provided in the Application.5 For brevity’s sake, those
analyses and inputs in Mr. Casey’s and the other Applicants witnesses testimony are not repeated
here.

        Mr. John Poole, the Commission Staff expert witness, also provided independent analyses
free from any routing preferences that might be based on his personal interests.6 Mr. Poole
examined the extensive amount of information provided in the Application, including the
Environmental Assessment, and also conducted his own analyses and reviewed testimony and
evidence provided by other parties in this docket; his recommendation is Route 487. Mr. is a
highly experienced engineer with a lengthy resume at the Commission, testifying in 38
transmission CCN cases (not counting this one),7 and previously serving in various professional
engineering roles. He is one of the most experienced engineering experts at the Commission, and
likely one of the most experienced planning professionals providing expert testimony in this case.

        While Mr. Poole acknowledged he did not have the time to review all the testimony filed
before his testimony was filed, he did his best to do so prior to his filing and continued to review
testimony and evidence after his testimony was filed - but by the time of the hearing on the merits
he had reviewed all the intervenor testimony.8 At the time he testified at the hearing, Mr. Poole
was exposed to more information in the course of his cross-examination. In the end, all the
additional information did not change his recommendation regarding the best route.9

                  A.       APPLICANTS “BEST MEETS” ROUTE 894

        Again, it is worth noting that Applicants have no vested interest in the location of the
transmission project, they are focused on compliance with applicable statutory and Commission
rule requirements. The route they recommend as the one that “best meets” those standards is Route
894. For brevity’s sake, the detailed analysis presented in support of Route 894 is not repeated
here but some features are worth mentioning.
        Many parties raise particular concerns about the degree of specific environmental impacts
are implicated by Route 894, such as in the Direct Testimony of Rae Lynn Schneider Reinecke on
behalf of Cherokee Creek Partners.10 While Route 894 is very strong on avoiding environmentally
sensitive areas, including endangered species habitat and otherwise positive regarding community
values, like all routing options there will be issues to resolve. To the degree those do exist,
Applicants have techniques and strategies to address them, including for construction in
endangered species habitat, environmentally sensitive stream segments (“ESSS”) in rivers and
streams, and karst terrain. Applicants’ expert witness Corin E. Cooley, testified that the Applicants
have considered these issues and how they would be addressed and their costs have already been
included as part of the cost estimate provided in the Application.11 As an example, when
challenged on whether the costs of additional construction techniques in karst terrain is employed
was included in cost estimates, Ms. Cooley responded that those additional costs had been included
in the overall costs estimate for affected route segments.12 Indeed, the track record for karst
mitigation is particularly positive as Ms. Cooley testified that to her knowledge there has been no
instances of karst or related aquifer contamination related to transmission tower construction.13

                 B.       COMMISISON STAFF “BEST MEETS” ROUTE 487

        Similarly, Mr. Poole conducted a very thorough analysis of the proposed routing options
with an open mind and a vast experience in transmission line routing evaluations. His reasoning
and conclusions are thoroughly documented in his testimony, and for brevity’s sake will not be
repeated here. However, his testimony summation of reasoning in support of his judgment that
Route 487 best meets statutory and Commission standards is worthy of a quote:

         I conclude that Route 487 best meets the criteria of PURA and the Commission’s rules
        because of but not limited to the following:
           (1) Route 487 is the 22nd least expensive proposed route at $2,060,282,000.00, a
           $28,582,000.00 or 1.41 % difference from the least expensive route;
           (2) Route 487 parallels or utilizes existing 1 compatible rights-of-way for 49.64% of its
           length which is the 4th most of any route;
           (3) Route 487 crosses no upland woodlands; and
           (4) Route 487 does not utilize Segment E6 which has 77 habitable structures within 500
           feet of its centerline.14

Mr. Poole acknowledges that there are still some shortcomings with the route (as there are with all
routes) but that in his seasoned judgment he considers “Route 487 overall to have the most
advantages and to be superior to the other proposed alternative routes.”15
        The conviction of this recommendation was affirmed regarding the discussion of Route
291, a route briefly mentioned in his May 29, 2026 deposition16 but for which he did not provide
any analysis about in his direct testimony – and indeed Mr. Poole continued to affirm that, even
after further review of the record, all testimony, analyses, and information presented in cross
examination, route 291 was, in his judgment, inferior to Route 487.17 Further, in the course of his
continued review and information elicited at the hearing on the merits, Mr. Poole acknowledged
there are additional concerns about Route 291 that further undermined his view of that route,
discussed more below.18

             II.     COMMON CHALLENGES FOR ALL ROUTES, SEGMENTS

        Throughout the direct testimony and the hearing of the merits, several alternative routes
were promoted by various parties in an obvious effort shift the transmission line route away from
their properties. This is of course an understandable strategy and one that could have merit. This
brief will not repeat those strategies and supporting testimony but only notes for now that each
have significant drawbacks and fail to overcome the superior character of Routes 894 and 487 in
meeting applicable standards.
        As is clear from the cross examination at the hearing on the merits, each of the alternatives
pressed by intervenors failed to achieve a level that surpasses the better choices of Route 894 and

questions attempting to undermine their recommendations. At the conclusion of their testimony,
the panel of witnesses for the Applicants, after almost two days of cross-examination, there was
no indication that the witnesses had changed their minds regarding their recommendation of Route
894, they remained committed to their judgment. Mr. Poole likewise affirmed his commitment to
his recommendation of Routh 487 as the best meets route in his judgment.19
          Parties opposing the judgment of Applicants’ experts and the Commission’s expert make
great efforts to find and press arguments to undermine these recommendations, rooted of course
in the same legal standards used by the Applicants and Commission Staff. Depending on their
preferred outcomes on routing, these intervenors emphasize some criteria over others. This, again,
is understandable. They also elicit specific facts about their particular properties, also to create
doubts about these independent evaluations. However, Mr. Poole rightly confirms that specific
issues, on particular properties, such as bifurcation of properties and more generally “community
values,” is really ubiquitous to all of the alternative routes presented in the Application,20 inferring
that weighing anecdotal conditions on one or a few segments should be done cautiously because
all routes and segments will have the same or similar conditions and concerns (the engagement of
resources to hire experts to ferret them out for a contested proceeding did not occur for those).

               III.    CHALLENGES FOR OTHER “ROUTES OF INTEREST”

          Several routes were advocated by parties for alternatives other than the routes
recommended by the Applicants and Commission Staff and were added to the highlighted as
“Routes of Interest” filed by the Applicants to help focus the review in this proceeding.21
Landowners are particularly concerned about proposals that would impact Segment i1, and indeed
find those proposals are greatly challenged and far less suitable than the “best meets”
recommendations of the Applicants and Commission Staff. This brief will forgo going into great
detail on these proposals, Landowners will have the opportunity to respond if indeed these parties
press their alternatives, but some highlights are useful as the ALJs conduct their review of the
record.

                  A.       Route 891 – Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed (Party 348)

        As a threshold matter, it should be noted that Route 891 was part of the original set of
potential routes identified by Applicants but not selected as part of the routes proposed in the
Application. As explained by Applicants’ witness Casey D. Petty, the Applicant initially identified
1,246 potential routes for the transmission line, set forth in Appendix D of the Application
Environmental Assessment, Table 7-1.22 From this large number of options, Applicants’ analyses
narrowed the options down to 122 routes as the most potentially compliant with state statutory
standards and Commission rules.23 Thus Route 891 did not even make this most basic cut for
consideration as the “best meets” route. In the analysis of the Applicants, a party disinterested in
the final route location, Route 891 came in – at best – at 123rd. This alone should disqualify this
route from further consideration, and decision-makers should not waste time and energy
considering it in this very time-compressed proceeding.
        The recommendation for Route 891 is provided by a witness unqualified to make such
recommendations in this proceeding. The witness, Karen Hubbard, conceded she is not: a qualified
routing consultant, wildlife biologist, anthropology, licensed in any field that provide expertise in
engineering design or viewshed analyses, or credentialed in any other related fields.24 And she
conceded that the only property that she conducted any analyses on or evaluation of was the
property of her clients, located on Segment G13 – and she did no analyses or evaluation on any
other properties either on that same segment (G13) nor any properties that would be affected by
her recommendation of Route 891.25 Ms. Hubbard also conceded that the routes she recommends,
inclusive of 891, impacts a greater number of habitable structures than Applicants’ recommended
Route: 108 to 173 within 500 feet vs. 85 for Route 894, and to which Ms. Hubbard admitted she
provided no additional analyses regarding impact to that larger number of habitations on her
recommended routes.26 Landowners urge that there be no further consideration of Route 891 as a
route that best meets applicable statutory and Commission requirement.

                  B.      Route 572 – Save the Lampasas (Party 391)

        Route 572 is recommended by witness Aaron Brewer. He relies upon a complex modeling
tool for which he does not reveal its mechanics or formulas and to which he only applied to a
limited number of routes and segments.27 The parties in the case, the ALJs, the Commission Staff
and the Commission itself has no way to evaluate or test the validity of Mr. Brewers methodology.
At a high level, it appears very suspect. At the hearing on the merits, Mr. Brewer admitted that
his recommended route is on its face scores lower on all manner of criteria for a suitable route,
including (as compared to Route 894) affecting 22 more habitable structures within 500 feet, is
greater cost, crosses more streams, has less paralleling of compatible right of way, more road
crossings, and other shortcomings readily apparent.28 Landowners urge that there be no further
consideration of Route 572 as a route that best meets applicable statutory and Commission
requirement.

                 C.      Route Cherokee G – Cherokee Creek, Segment K13/K51 (Parties 474,
                 551)

        This route, contrived by this group of parties, sponsored by witness Rae Lynn Schneider
Reinecke,29 was not proposed as an alternative route in the Application. Therefore, neither the
public nor the parties were provided notice that this particular route could be considered in this
proceeding as an alterative path for the project. As such it should rejected entirely in this
proceeding. Other parties will address this legal issue as well, so that detailed briefing will not be
repeated here.
        In addition, Ms. Reinecke testified that her analyses were unconcerned about project costs
and she affirmed has no expertise in engineering.30 Not surprisingly, the resulting contrived route,
pieced together segments of her choosing, comes in at a staggering additional cost of $73,687,644
million as compared to Route 894.31 The route also has 20 more habitable structures, 41 more
transmission towers, and is substantially longer than Routh 894.32 This proposed route, while

been included as part of the cost estimate provided in the Application.34 Landowners urge that

                 D.      Route 296 - Commission Staff

        As discussed above, Mr. Poole mentioned Route 296 briefly in his May 29, 2026
deposition.35 However, Mr. Poole did not offer any analysis about this route in his direct
testimony, as opposed to his extensive analysis explaining his judgment that Route 487 is the “best
meets” route, and indeed Mr. Poole continued to affirm that, even after further review of the record,
analyses, and information presented in cross examination, Route 296 was, in his judgment, inferior
to Route 487.36       Further, in the course of his continued review of testimony and information
elicited at the hearing on the merits, Mr. Poole acknowledged there are additional concerns about
Route 296 that further undermined his view of that route.37 A particular example is the existence
of an elementary school, Florence Elementary School, that is located on Segment J34, that had not
been previously identified in the Application, which he admitted was a significant factor.38 For
these reasons, this route should be rejected as a candidate for the “best meets” route in this
proceeding.

                 E.      Route WBW 2-1 – Whitis Land Investments LP (Party 34)

        In addition, in his direct testimony, Mr. Whitis asserts that “using the information provided
we were able to infer projected costs, and many customer routes were submitted to the Applicants
through an RFI. We have not received the Applicants’ response, so our estimates are provided
below.” 40 As to other routes Mr. Whitis pieced together, labeled WBW 1-9, WBW 1-19, WBW
1-6, WBW 1-20, and WBW 1-15, this statement appears to be true as to seeking RFIs on those
routes (the RFI responses were not offered at hearing).41 However, Mr. Whitis admitted at the
hearing on the merits that he had not submitted the RFI regarding his Route WBW 2-1,42 clearly
indicating his lack of conviction to this proposal. Mr. Whitis testified that he has no credentials as
an expert in any applicable expertise regarding line routing.43 And he further confirmed he
conducted no analysis on any properties other than his own, and that his sole objective was to keep
the transmission line off of his properties.44 Based on these facts, Landowners urge the ALJs
disregard Mr. Whitis’ recommendation regarding his proposed Route WBW 2-1.

                  IV.      PARTICULAR UNSUITABILITY OF SEGMENT I1

        Finally, Landowners affirm their testimony, by Marylynne Norman47 and Steve Lazar,48
that Segment i1 has particular features that make the segment unsuitable for transmission line
development. In addition, although Landowners understand that this process is not a “popularity
contest,” it is highly relevant that virtually all landowners affected by Segment i1 have intervened
in opposition to the proposed segment, as evidenced by Applicants’ Intervenor Map.49

                         I.      DISINTERESTED PARTIES ON ROUTE

        The record in this case will surely be one of the most voluminous in the history of SOAH
with literally thousands of filings in the docket inclusive of several hundred sets of testimony and
other filings and other documents that landed in the evidentiary record. This along with the
extraordinarily short timeframe the ALJs must meet to provide the Commission a Proposal for
Decision ("PFD") in time for a Commission decision by September 22,2026, will be an immense
and unprecedented task.          Of course, transmission line CCN proceedings are notoriously
contentious as landowners and those that live in the areas affected by new transmission lines are
very motivated to prevent these proj ects from coming into their communities. Not to mention that
many other factors that must be considered such as environmental impacts, affects to community
values, and impacts to sites of historic and prehistoric significance.

        The intervenors advocating for a particular route in this case are motivated by their interest
and preference to not have a transmission line located on or near them.                 This is certainly an
understandable motivation for engagement in this process, but it must be acknowledged there is
an inherent bias in the advocacy for the ultimate route selection in the recommendation by the
ALJs . However , there are two parties that are solely motivated by the legal obligation to comply
with the requirements and standards set forth in the Public Utility Regulatory Act ("PURA") and
Commission's rules.2 Those are the Applicants and the Commission Staff.
